Volume 06 · Chapter 07

Inflation, expectations and nominal rigidity

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c06

By the endExplain inflation dynamics and distinguish supply from demand disturbances.

Explain the rate of price change without confusing the levels

Capability: explain inflation dynamics and distinguish supply from demand disturbances. Prerequisite: money, banking and monetary transmission, especially the distinction between deposits and reserves and the timing of nominal versus real returns. We use log changes, expectations and simultaneous equations from earlier volumes. A higher price level, faster inflation, a higher relative energy price and an unexpected price increase are four different statements. A useful account of inflation begins by specifying which statement the evidence supports.

All numerical examples and model shocks below are original synthetic constructions. A period is a common decision interval unless an exercise explicitly calls it a quarter. No parameter is estimated from actual inflation data. Historical method sources support the economic distinctions; the chapter's small pricing model is a maintained teaching mechanism, not a fully derived general equilibrium model or a prediction for October 2026.

Price indices, ordinary inflation and exact compounding

Let Pt > 0 be the price of a specified composite good in currency per unit, or a consistently normalized index proportional to that price. Ordinary net inflation over t−1 to t is πgt = Pt/Pt−1−1, with domain πgt > −1. Multiplying by 100 expresses this rate as a percentage. An index's base normalization changes its reported level, not this ratio. Indices with different baskets, expenditure coverage or index-number methods can measure different inflation rates; revisit national-account measurement before comparing them.

Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a negative inflation rate. If an index rises from 100 to 110 to 115.5, inflation falls from 10% to 5% while the level continues upward. The cumulative increase is 15.5%, since 1.10×1.05 = 1.155. Returning inflation to a target does not return the price level to its earlier path. A one-time relative-price change can affect a measured index in the adjustment period; continued inflation at the same rate requires further aggregate price increases.

Over several periods, PT/P₀ = ∏t=1T(1+πgt). A quarterly rate q annualizes to (1+q)⁴−1 if it repeats for four quarters. Multiplying q by four is only an approximation, not an observed annual change. Report the horizon and whether a rate is annualized.

For the linear model later, define pt = 100 ln Pt, using fixed price units, and Πt = pt−pt−1 = 100 ln(Pt/Pt−1). Π is measured in log points per period. Conversion is exact: πg = exp(Π/100)−1. Thus Π = 3 means ordinary inflation of approximately 3.045%, not exactly 3%. Log changes add across periods. Ordinary percentage changes do not.

A nominal net interest rate it is contracted at t for t to t+1. If its payoff is certain in currency, the realized gross return in goods is

1+rt+1 = (1+it)Pt/Pt+1 = (1+it)/(1+πgt+1),   it > −1.

Hence 100 ln(1+rt+1) = 100 ln(1+it)−Πt+1. Subtraction of ordinary rates, r ≈ i−πg, is first order only. Before inflation is realized, the exact expected gross return is (1+it)Et[1/(1+πgt+1)], assuming it is integrable. It generally differs from (1+it)/(1+Etπgt+1). An expected return is also not a risk-adjusted Euler-equation discount rate. Unexpected inflation changes the real value of a fixed nominal promise; indexation, default and taxes would alter the contract comparison.

MV = PY is an identity until a causal model is supplied

Choose a monetary aggregate Mt > 0 measured as the average nominal money stock over period t, in currency units. Let Yt > 0 be real final output per period and Pt its corresponding deflator, so PtYt is nominal output per period. Define income velocity Vt = PtYt/Mt, with units inverse periods. Then MtVt = PtYt holds by construction. Defining velocity this way does not measure a literal common turnover speed for every unit of money, and this income identity does not count every financial or intermediate transaction.

Let μt, vt and gt be the ordinary growth rates of M, V and Y between adjacent equal-length periods. Dividing the identities gives the exact growth relation

1+πgt = (1+μt)(1+vt)/(1+gt).

Equivalently, Πt = 100Δln Mt+100Δln Vt−100Δln Yt. The familiar πg ≈ μ+v−g drops product and compounding terms. None of these accounting statements tells us which variable responds when policy changes.

A simple quantity-theory prediction adds substantive restrictions: the specified M is set by an exogenous policy intervention; money demand implies a stable V that does not respond to that intervention over the comparison; real output is fixed by real determinants at the horizon; and nominal prices can adjust to clear markets. Under those restrictions P = MV/Y, so a proportional change in M induces the same proportional price-level change. If M grows persistently while V is constant and Y grows at g, sustained ordinary inflation is (1+μ)/(1+g)−1. A single permanent level increase in M instead produces a one-time price adjustment, with no further inflation from that increase alone.

The restrictions can fail in the short run or under a changed regime. Interest rates, payment technology and desired liquidity can alter velocity; credit demand and bank lending can make a monetary aggregate endogenous; real output can respond; prices may be predetermined. Central-bank reserves and broad deposits are different stocks. Increasing reserves does not, by this identity, imply a proportional increase in broad money or prices. A stable historical correlation also does not establish invariance to a new intervention.

Fisher's The Purchasing Power of Money, chapter II §§2, 4–5, derives an equation for transaction expenditure and explicitly conditions proportional price changes on unchanged velocity and quantities. The linked text is the 1922 second-edition presentation of a work first published in 1911. Our income-velocity definition uses final output rather than silently equating Fisher's transaction volume with GDP.

Worked example 1: the same money growth, different inflation

Initially M₀ = 100 currency units, V₀ = 2 per period and Y₀ = 200 goods per period, giving P₀ = 1 currency unit per good. Next period M₁ = 108 and Y₁ = 204. If V₁ stays at 2, nominal output is 216 and P₁ = 216/204 = 18/17. Inflation is 1/17, approximately 5.882%, rather than the first-order calculation 8%−2% = 6%.

But if V₁ = 17/9, nominal output is 108(17/9) = 204 and P₁ = 1, giving zero inflation with the same money growth and real-output growth. The identity accommodates both cases. A causal forecast must justify the velocity response. Neither scenario is an observation about an actual country.

In the first scenario, a date-0 nominal loan of 100 paying 108 at date 1 has an 8% nominal return. It buys 100 goods initially and 108/(18/17) = 102 goods at repayment, an exact 2% real return. Subtracting 5.882% from 8% would overstate it. If 8% money growth and 2% output growth repeat with constant velocity, the 1/17 inflation rate repeats; if only the money level changes once, that conclusion does not follow.

A transparent nominal-rigidity mechanism

A nominal rigidity restricts the adjustment of prices or wages in currency terms. It need not mean no observed price ever changes. Contracts, costly re-optimization or infrequent information can generate different adjustment mechanisms. We now solve one deliberately narrow mechanism so that its expectation date and aggregate feedback are visible.

Take a continuum of small price setters. Fraction s ∈ (0,1) sets its period-t log price in advance at qpret = pt−1+et. Here et is a forecast of Πt formed with information through t−1; it is not a forecast of Πt+1 made at t. The remaining fraction can reset after current disturbances are observed. A resetting firm chooses its log price q to minimize the maintained quadratic loss

ℓ(q) = ½[q−(pt+a xt+zt)]²,   a > 0.

Every log price is 100 times a natural logarithm. Output gap xt = 100 ln(Yt/Ȳt) is in log points; a is log-price points per output-gap log point; and zt is a cost/desired-markup disturbance in log-price points. Loss is in squared log points, not currency profit or social welfare. Ȳt is a supplied reference-output path for baseline real conditions, held fixed in a shock comparison. A disturbance can change the shock-specific flexible-price allocation, so x is not automatically the gap to that allocation or a measure of welfare loss.

Each small resetting firm treats aggregate pt, xt and zt as given. Its unique global minimizer is qresett = pt+a xt+zt, since the squared loss is nonnegative and zero there. This target and the preset rule are assumptions, not a derivation from a complete consumer-demand and production system.

Define the aggregate price index to be the geometric weighted index of these two groups. Taking logs gives pt = s qpret+(1−s)qresett. Substituting the two prices and collecting the aggregate price on both sides gives the fixed-point restriction

s(pt−pt−1−et) = (1−s)(a xt+zt).

For 0 < s < 1, divide by s to obtain an expectations-augmented Phillips relation:

Πt = et+κxt+ut,   κ = (1−s)a/s > 0,   ut = (1−s)zt/s.

Higher activity raises desired relative prices; predetermined prices make surprise aggregate inflation accompany activity above the reference path. The shock u is the scaled pricing disturbance, not an unemployment rate. This is an exact equation within our log-index model. It is not an empirical regression or the forward-looking New Keynesian Phillips curve. Wage-setting models can yield other inflation–activity relations; converting an output gap into an unemployment gap requires an additional labor-market relation, not a change of labels.

Handle endpoints in the undivided equation. If s = 1, all prices are preset and Π = e; current output or z cannot change current inflation through this mechanism. If s = 0, all reset and a x+z = 0. Aggregate pricing alone no longer determines the nominal price level: demand must supply the nominal anchor. In particular, do not insert s = 0 into κ or hold u fixed while changing s and call z unchanged.

Christian Wolf's MIT 14.05 Lecture 19: Sticky Prices (Fall 2025) develops nominal/real returns, price-setting and an adjustment-cost route from marginal costs to inflation. Its pricing environment is richer and different from our preset/reset construction. It provides a route toward deriving a Phillips relation from firm choices; our quadratic target, geometric index and one-period preset rule do not constitute that full microfoundation.

Close the model before comparing shocks

The Phillips relation alone has two endogenous quantities, Π and x. Close the period-t model with a stated aggregate-demand schedule

xt = dt−b(Πt−Π*),   b > 0.

Π* is a fixed log-inflation anchor; d is a demand intercept in output-gap log points; b is output-gap log points per log-inflation point. For a given previous price, higher current inflation means a higher current price, reducing real spending under this schedule. The slope summarizes a maintained spending/policy regime, not an estimated universal response or a claim that every interest-rate regime behaves this way.

For b = 1 there is a simple exact nominal-expenditure implementation. Define nominal expenditure Nt by 100 ln Nt = pt−1+100 ln Ȳt+Π*+dt and require Nt = PtYt. Subtraction gives x = d−(Π−Π*). The chosen expenditure target is the behavioral/policy restriction; the equality N = PY alone is not. Other b values need their own demand mechanism, such as spending responses combined with a policy rule. Business-cycle models will develop those closures.

For 0 < s < 1, substitution gives the unique simultaneous solution because 1+κb > 0:

Π = [e+κd+κbΠ*+u]/(1+κb),   x = [d−b(e−Π*)−bu]/(1+κb).

Holding the other primitives fixed, ∂Π/∂d = κ/(1+κb) > 0 and ∂x/∂d = 1/(1+κb) > 0. A demand expansion raises inflation and activity. A positive pricing disturbance instead gives ∂Π/∂u = 1/(1+κb) > 0 and ∂x/∂u = −b/(1+κb) < 0. A higher predetermined e also raises current inflation and reduces x under this closure. These are model comparative statics, conditional on the reference path and regime.

With s = 1, use Π = e and x = d−b(e−Π*). With s = 0, x = −z/a and Π = Π*+(d+z/a)/b. All prices and output levels recovered by exponentiation remain positive, but that does not make large log deviations economically credible. The linear target and demand schedule are a local teaching specification; extrapolation requires a model of capacity, substitution, nonlinear costs and changing behavior.

Worked example 2: demand expansion versus a pricing disturbance

Set s = 2/3, a = 1, b = 1 and e = Π* = 2. Thus κ = 1/2, u = z/2 and 1+κb = 3/2. The baseline d = z = 0 gives x = 0 and Π = 2. A demand expansion d = 3 with z = 0 gives x = 3/(3/2) = 2 and Π = 2+(1/2)2 = 3. Ordinary inflation is exp(0.03)−1, about 3.045%; output is exp(0.02)−1, about 2.020%, above the reference level.

Instead set d = 0 and z = 6, so u = 3. Then x = −3/(3/2) = −2 and Π = 2−1+3 = 4. Inflation rises while activity falls. With pt−1 = 0, the preset log price is 2 and reset log price is p+x+z = 4−2+6 = 8. Their geometric-index log average is (2/3)2+(1/3)8 = 4, confirming the aggregate fixed point.

The same inflation Π = 3 from the demand case could instead arise with d = 0 and u = 3/2, giving x = −1. Inflation alone cannot distinguish these cases. If the adverse disturbance is u = 3 and e remains 2, holding Π at 2 would require x = −6 and d = −6; holding x at zero would instead require Π = 5 and d = 3. The two targets cannot both be met through d alone in that period. Choosing between them requires a welfare objective and feasible policy instruments that this comparison has not supplied.

Expectations, disinflation and stability

An adaptive forecast uses forecast errors to update: et+1 = et+λ(Πt−et), where 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1. It uses realized period-t inflation only when forecasting period t+1. At λ = 1 the next forecast equals the latest realization; at λ = 0 it never changes. This is a behavioral forecasting rule. Calling it adaptive does not establish that it is statistically optimal or how actual expectations are formed.

For constant κ > 0, b > 0, anchor Π*, and d = u = 0 after a regime change, define Et = et−Π*. The equilibrium gives Πt−Π* = Et/(1+κb) and xt = −bEt/(1+κb). Substituting into the update yields

Et+1 = ρEt,   ρ = 1−λκb/(1+κb).

For 0 < λ ≤ 1, 0 < ρ < 1, so Et = ρtE₀ converges monotonically to zero. The price level still accumulates the inflation realizations; convergence of inflation is not convergence to an old price-level path. If λ = 0, ρ = 1 and a nonzero initial forecast error persists. At the fully preset boundary κ = 0, Π = e and this update cannot move expectations. At b = 0, outside the maintained demand-response domain, x = d: with d = u = 0 any e is stationary. Expectations adjustment alone therefore does not guarantee target convergence; the pricing and demand feedbacks matter.

For constant nonzero d and u, the update instead is Et+1 = ρEt+λ(κd+u)/(1+κb). With λ, κ and b positive, its fixed point is E* = (κd+u)/(κb). Subtracting E* proves convergence with the same ρ. Long-run x* = −u/κ and Π = e = Π*+E*. Thus the zero-shock stability result cannot be reused without accounting for a persistent forcing term.

Worked example 3: a disinflation path conditional on slow learning

Keep κ = 1/2 and b = 1; let λ = 1/2 and Π* = 2. Following a change in the maintained regime, initial e₀ = 4 remains above the anchor and dt = ut = 0 thereafter. Then ρ = 1−(1/2)(1/2)/(3/2) = 5/6. At t = 0, Π₀ = 2+2/(3/2) = 10/3 and x₀ = −4/3. The next forecast is e₁ = 4+(1/2)(10/3−4) = 11/3. Then Π₁ = 2+(5/3)/(3/2) = 28/9 and x₁ = −10/9.

In general et = 2+2(5/6)t and xt = −(4/3)(5/6)t. The infinite sum of gap deviations is −(4/3)/(1−5/6) = −8 log-point-periods. This is an exact sum of model log gaps, not eight units of lost goods, an estimated sacrifice ratio or a social-welfare cost. Converting to cumulative output quantities needs the reference path and exp(x/100)−1; welfare also needs preferences and other distortions. Different expectation adjustment or policy would change the path.

Under the special rule et = Πt−1, the Phillips relation becomes Πt−Πt−1 = κxt+ut. With u = 0, sustaining a positive x requires ever-increasing log inflation, not simply a permanently high constant inflation rate. Doing so would also require changing the demand intercept over time, rather than silently keeping the earlier closure fixed. This acceleration statement is conditional on that forecasting rule and pricing relation; it is not a law that every economy must obey.

Friedman's The Role of Monetary Policy (1968), the employment discussion on printed pages 8–11, emphasizes anticipated versus realized nominal changes and challenges a permanently exploitable inflation–unemployment trade-off. We use that distinction, not the paper's historical numerical claims or policy prescription. Our adaptive coefficient, convergence speed and cumulative-gap calculation are original assumptions and deductions.

Model-consistent forecasts are not perfect foresight

Under a different expectation assumption, et = E[Πt | It−1], with the conditional distribution generated by this same model, known parameters and policy regime. For simplicity all shocks below have finite support, so expectations exist. This is model-consistent or rational expectations within the maintained model; it does not mean forecasters see tomorrow's shock or that the model has been empirically verified.

Taking the conditional expectation of the solved inflation equation and using e = EΠ gives κb(e−Π*) = κE[d|I]+E[u|I]. Therefore

e = Π* + [κE(d|I)+E(u|I)]/(κb),   κ,b > 0.

If both conditional shock means are zero, e = Π*. With equally probable demand surprises d = −3 and d = 3, u = 0 and the baseline parameters, outcomes are (x,Π) = (−2,1) and (2,3). Expected Π is 2, yet realized forecast errors are −1 and +1. Because Π is log inflation, exp(EΠ/100)−1 is not generally E[πg]. The forecast's variable and units must be named.

If instead d = 3 is known before prices are preset and u = 0, the consistent forecast is e = 2+3 = 5. Equilibrium then has Π = 5 and x = 0. The same sized realized demand intercept produced Π = 3 and x = 2 when it was a surprise to presetters. Information timing changes the comparison. The result does not prove that every anticipated policy has no real effect: this model omits many taxes, financing frictions, multi-period contracts and real distortions through which it could act. A policy announcement also need not be believed merely because it was announced.

Future-looking pricing models often contain EtΠt+1. That object differs from our predetermined forecast Et−1Πt. Replacing one with the other changes the system and usually requires a terminal or equilibrium-selection condition. The next chapter solves a bounded forward-looking system; graduate macroeconomics develops its microfoundations and longer-horizon analysis.

From a shock story to an identification argument

With known κ, b, Π*, e and a reliable x, the model can recover d = x+b(Π−Π*) and u = Π−e−κx. That is a decomposition conditional on the equations, not independent evidence that the recovered disturbances are exogenous causal forces. Potential/reference output is not directly observed, expectations vary across people and dates, and policy can respond to the same news that moves private demand.

Even observing Π and x may leave ambiguity. The baseline demand case (Π,x) = (3,2) is consistent with e = 2, u = 0 or with e = 1, u = 1, keeping d = 3. A measured forecast could help distinguish these explanations, but its information date, population, horizon and measurement error matter. A single rising input price is likewise not a complete explanation of a persistent aggregate inflation process: the basket weight, pass-through, substitution, other shocks, expectations and policy response enter.

Nor is an unconditional scatterplot a structural Phillips curve. In our model demand-only shocks move observations along the pricing relation, while pricing shocks shift it and move activity in the opposite direction. Simultaneous shocks, changing reference output or a changing policy regime can obscure either pattern. Estimating the response to an identified disturbance requires a design: for example, a justified external instrument or unexpected event, with a clear timing and exclusion argument, appropriate outcomes, uncertainty and robustness. It is not enough to label an inflation residual “supply” after seeing its sign.

The synthetic inputs, standard-library benchmark, preserved exact output and README reproduce the model comparisons, including the pricing endpoints. The code performs conditional arithmetic; it estimates no empirical slope and identifies no actual shock.

Exercises

  1. An index moves from 100 to 110 to 115.5 in consecutive quarters. Compute both quarterly rates, the cumulative rate and the annualized rate if the second quarterly rate repeats. Distinguish disinflation from deflation. Separately, a certain nominal gross return is 11/10 and next-period ordinary inflation is 0 or 1/5 with equal probability. Compute the exact expected real gross return and compare it with using mean inflation in the denominator.
  2. Money grows 10%, velocity falls 2% and real output grows 4%. Derive exact inflation from MV = PY and compare the first-order calculation. State the extra restrictions needed to infer a causal effect of an exogenous monetary expansion, and explain why an expansion of reserves is not automatically the same intervention.
  3. Derive the aggregate pricing fixed point. With s = 3/4, a = 3/2, z = 2, e = 1, x = 2 and previous log price zero, calculate κ, u, Π and both group prices. Verify the index directly. State the distinct restrictions at s = 0 and s = 1.
  4. Using κ = 1/2, b = 2, e = Π* = 2, d = 4 and u = 1, solve both equilibrium quantities and verify both equations. Derive the demand and pricing-shock derivatives. For the worked cost disturbance u = 3 with b = 1 and e = Π* = 2, compare the demand intercept required to hold inflation at 2 with that required to hold x at zero. Can both targets be met?
  5. Prove the adaptive recursion and its stability conditions. At κ = 1/2, b = 1, λ = 1, Π* = 2, e₀ = 5 and zero disturbances, find ρ, the first two inflation/gap pairs and the infinite cumulative log gap. Discuss λ = 0. If d = 3 and u = 0 instead persist, derive the limiting e, Π and x.
  6. Derive the model-consistent forecast for conditional shock means. Recompute the equally probable d = ±3 case and the known d = 3 case at the baseline parameters. Why can rational forecasts be wrong when realized, and why is knowing a realized policy change insufficient to classify it as a surprise?
  7. Give two different shock cases producing Π = 3 in the worked model and explain what activity data add. Then compute the descriptive intercept-OLS slope of Π on x for two equally likely demand-only states d = ±3, and separately for two equally likely pricing-only states u = ±3, with e = Π* = 2, κ = 1/2 and b = 1. Compute the slope in a four-state mixture assigning probability 1/4 to each of these states. Is any disagreement with κ an arithmetic contradiction?
  8. A memo says: “Money increased, inflation fell, so quantity accounting is false. Prices rose while output fell, proving a supply shock. An announced disinflation has no output cost because expectations are rational.” Evaluate each sentence. Propose a concise empirical plan specifying the price index, money aggregate, timing, activity benchmark, expectation measure and identification assumptions. Distinguish verifying accounting, estimating a conditional model and identifying a policy effect.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The rates are 110/100−1 = 10% and 115.5/110−1 = 5%. The cumulative rate is 15.5%; the repeated-quarter annualized rate is 1.05⁴−1 = 0.21550625, or 21.550625%, not 20%. Inflation is positive but falls, so this is disinflation without deflation. The price level has not returned to 100. In the separate return problem, expected real gross return is (1/2)(11/10)+(1/2)(11/12) = 121/120. The expected net return is 1/120, about 0.8333%. Mean ordinary inflation is 1/10, so substituting it into the denominator gives (11/10)/(11/10) = 1, incorrectly implying zero expected net return. Averaging a reciprocal differs from taking the reciprocal of an average.

  2. Dividing the two identities yields 1+πg = (11/10)(49/50)/(26/25) = 539/520. Thus πg = 19/520, approximately 3.65385%. The first-order answer is 10%−2%−4% = 4%, an overstatement of about 0.34615 percentage points. A proportional causal price prediction requires a well-defined exogenous change in the chosen M, a velocity/money-demand response held invariant, real output unaffected at the comparison horizon and price adjustment consistent with equilibrium. These restrictions do not follow from the identity. Reserves are bank/central-bank balance-sheet items distinct from the chosen public monetary aggregate; no fixed conversion into broad deposits or expenditure has been established.

  3. Substitution gives p = s(pprev+e)+(1−s)(p+a x+z), hence s(Π−e) = (1−s)(a x+z). For interior s, κ = [(1/4)/(3/4)](3/2) = 1/2 and u = [(1/4)/(3/4)]2 = 2/3. Then Π = 1+(1/2)2+2/3 = 8/3. The preset log price is 1 and the reset log price is 8/3+3+2 = 23/3. Their weighted mean is (3/4)1+(1/4)(23/3) = 8/3, exactly the aggregate log price. These are log prices; the actual group prices are exp(1/100) and exp(23/300) in the chosen units. At s = 0 the restriction is a x+z = 0 and nominal demand must pin down inflation. At s = 1 it is Π = e. Division by s is invalid at zero.

  4. The denominator is 1+(1/2)2 = 2. Output gap is [4−2(2−2)−2]/2 = 1 and inflation is 2+(1/2)1+1 = 7/2. Demand verifies 4−2(7/2−2) = 1. The derivatives are Πd = κ/(1+κb), xd = 1/(1+κb), Πu = 1/(1+κb) and xu = −b/(1+κb). They describe a single disturbance with other primitives fixed. In the separate worked cost case, Π = 2 implies 2 = 2+(1/2)x+3, so x = −6 and demand needs d = −6. Holding x = 0 instead gives Π = 5 and d = 3. The same d cannot implement both: the pricing relation rules out (Π,x) = (2,0) when e = 2, u = 3. Selecting a policy requires objectives and feasibility, not just these derivatives.

  5. Zero shocks imply Π−Π* = (e−Π*)/(1+κb). Inserting this into enext = (1−λ)e+λΠ gives Enext = [1−λκb/(1+κb)]E. For positive κ,b and 0 < λ ≤ 1 the bracket is strictly between zero and one, so iteration proves monotone convergence. Here ρ = 2/3. Initially Π₀ = 2+3/(3/2) = 4 and x₀ = −2; e₁ = Π₀ = 4 then gives Π₁ = 10/3 and x₁ = −4/3. The gap sum is −2/(1−2/3) = −6 log-point-periods. At λ = 0, the initial e remains 5 forever, Π remains 4 and x remains −2; there is no finite infinite sum. With d = 3, u = 0 persisting and λ > 0, the forced fixed point is e−2 = (κ3)/(κb) = 3, so e = Π = 5 and x = 0. The unchanged contraction factor proves convergence to that shifted fixed point, not to the original anchor.

  6. Taking prior-information expectations of (1+κb)Π = e+κd+κbΠ*+u and using EΠ = e yields κb(e−Π*) = κE d+E u. Division by positive κb gives the displayed forecast. With zero conditional means, e = 2. The demand states −3 and +3 give (x,Π) = (−2,1) and (2,3), respectively. Their average inflation is 2 and each realized forecast error is nonzero. If d = 3 is known in advance, e = 5, Π = 5 and x = 0. Model consistency restricts conditional average forecast errors, not every realized error. The announcement, market information and preset-price dates must be observed or justified: a policy change can be anticipated before its formal announcement, or an announcement can be untrusted. Changing the information set changes this comparison.

  7. Demand d = 3, u = 0 gives Π = 3,x = 2; pricing disturbance d = 0, u = 3/2 gives Π = 3,x = −1. A reliable x distinguishes these particular pure-shock cases conditional on known e, slopes and reference output. It does not validate those assumptions. For the demand-only pair, (x,Π) = (−2,1),(2,3), giving mean x = 0, mean Π = 2, covariance 2 and variance of x equal to 4; the OLS slope is 1/2. For the pricing-only pair, (x,Π) = (2,0),(−2,4), the covariance is −4 and variance is 4, so the slope is −1. In the four-state mixture, covariance is (2−4)/2 = −1 and variance remains 4, giving slope −1/4. Every observation satisfies the same structural κ = 1/2 equation, but u covaries with x in the pricing cases. The descriptive regression mixes movements along and shifts of the pricing relation. No contradiction, and no empirical slope, has been produced.

  8. The first sentence confuses an identity with a behavioral restriction: velocity, output or measurement coverage can change while MV = PY continues to hold. The second treats one conditional sign pattern as unique identification; mixed shocks, changing expectations, reference-output error and endogenous policy responses can also matter. The third converts a result of one timing/model experiment into a universal claim. Rational expectations do not remove all contract, finance or real distortions, guarantee belief in an announcement or reveal the information set.

    A strong plan names the index/basket and observation vintage, uses a matching nominal-output deflator when checking income velocity, specifies the public monetary aggregate separately from reserves, aligns periods and rate conventions, and records the output/reference series and uncertainty in its construction. It measures dated inflation expectations for a relevant population and horizon, documents price-setting and policy timing, and states competing demand, cost and expectation channels before estimation. A policy-effect study needs a justified comparison or instrument with relevance, exclusion/exogeneity and anticipation assumptions, uncertainty and prespecified robustness. Reproducing accounting verifies arithmetic; fitting a conditional equation describes its sample; identifying a policy effect requires the counterfactual design. Other concrete plans receive credit when these distinctions are respected.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain why a fall in inflation need not lower prices, why MV = PY cannot by itself predict an intervention, and why an unchanged structural Phillips relation can generate opposite observed inflation–activity slopes. A complete explanation defines the rate/horizon, names the behavioral restrictions and expectation date, and gives a concrete demand-versus-pricing comparison.

Delayed check: with κ = b = 1 and e = Π* = 2, solve a surprise d = 2, u = 0. Next, set d = u = 0, λ = 1/2 and initial e₀ = 4; give ρ, the first two inflation realizations and the cumulative log gap. Finally find the exact real net return for nominal i = 5% and realized ordinary inflation of 2%.

Delayed-check answers

The surprise gives x = 1 and Π = 3 log points, so ordinary inflation is exp(0.03)−1. The adaptive experiment has ρ = 3/4; Π₀ = 3, x₀ = −1, e₁ = 7/2 and Π₁ = 11/4. The cumulative gap is −1/(1−3/4) = −4 log-point-periods. The exact real net return is (21/20)/(51/50)−1 = 1/34, about 2.94118%, rather than exactly 3%.

Next: business cycles and stabilization models develops alternative demand closures and a finite forward-looking model. Preserve the distinction between its forecast EtΠt+1 and the preset-price forecast used here.

Sources and further study

  • Irving Fisher, assisted by Harry G. Brown — The Purchasing Power of Money, second-edition text (1922; first published 1911), chapter II — Original equation-of-exchange derivation and explicit unchanged-velocity/quantity conditions; distinguishes the source's transaction aggregate from the chapter's defined income velocity.
  • Christian Wolf — MIT 14.05 Intermediate Macroeconomics, Lecture 19: Sticky Prices (Fall 2025) — Exact nominal/real gross-return timing and a primary university route from price-setting/adjustment costs through marginal costs to inflation; scope comparison with the original preset/reset teaching model.
  • Milton Friedman — The Role of Monetary Policy (American Economic Review, March 1968) — Anticipated versus realized nominal changes, temporary adjustment and the critique of a permanent exploitable inflation–unemployment trade-off.
